about.heading: About Me (&) My Journey
about.intro: I started out wanting to know why some sites pull traffic for free while others pay for every visitor and still go unseen. Thirty-odd websites later, that is still the question I open every project with.

cards.heading: Marketing, from the ground up
cards.short: BBA Marketing at IMSciences, Peshawar. Four years on consumer behaviour, brand strategy and what actually makes people buy.
cards.long: I read BBA Marketing at the Institute of Management Sciences in Peshawar. Consumer behaviour, brand strategy, market research, the fundamentals. It taught me to think about buyers before channels, and that habit has served me better than any tool I have picked up since.

cards.heading: What makes people trust a website
cards.short: Research on consumer trust in e-commerce, and how perceived risk quietly decides what people are willing to buy.
cards.long: My research looked at consumer trust in e-commerce and how it shapes online purchasing, using the PROCESS macro and a Sobel test to isolate perceived risk as a mediating variable. Dry work on paper. It also changed how I read a conversion rate for good, because the number on its own never tells you what the visitor was worried about.

cards.heading: First audits, first surprises
cards.short: Most sites are not held back by their writing. They are held back by things nobody has looked at in a year.
cards.long: The first proper audits I ran taught me a pattern I still see every month. Everyone assumes the content is the problem. It rarely is. It is a redirect chain nobody noticed, forty pages sharing one meta title, a robots rule left over from staging. Unglamorous, and usually the reason nothing is moving.

cards.heading: The unglamorous half
cards.short: Technical SEO at UnitedSol. Crawl paths, redirect chains, schema, indexation. None of it looks like marketing.
cards.long: At UnitedSol I went deep on the technical side. Crawl budget, indexation gaps, redirect chains, schema, page speed. This is where the compounding lives, and it is also the work nobody puts in a client update. Fix it once and everything you publish afterwards works harder for you.

cards.heading: Seven sites, seven problems
cards.short: Google Ads and SEO at DX Creativ. Seven live client sites, every one broken in a different way.
cards.long: At DX Creativ I ran SEO across seven live client websites at once, covering technical audits, on-page work, content strategy and link-building oversight, with Google Ads search campaigns running alongside. Seven sites at seven different stages will teach you prioritisation faster than any course. There is never time to fix everything, so you learn to find the one change that moves the most.

cards.heading: Paid and organic, same system
cards.short: Performance marketing at Remote Opus. Ads and SEO stopped being two separate jobs.
cards.long: At Remote Opus I own performance marketing end to end. Google and Meta Ads, SEO, landing pages, conversion tracking. Running both sides showed me how much gets wasted by keeping them apart. Paid tells you inside a fortnight which keywords bring buyers rather than browsers, and that is the most useful input an organic strategy can have.

cards.heading: Still the same question
cards.short: What is actually stopping this site from growing? Everything I do follows from the answer.
cards.long: The method has not changed since that first audit. Find what is broken, rank it by what it costs you, fix the expensive things first, then build content and campaigns around what buyers are already typing into Google. No templates, no guesswork, and no reporting that quietly hides a bad month.

items.q: How long before I see results?
items.a: Technical fixes can show movement in weeks. Content and authority take months. Most projects show something measurable in Search Console between six and twelve weeks, and the real gains compound after that. If someone promises you page one in thirty days, they are selling you something.

items.q: Do you work on paid ads as well as SEO?
items.a: Yes, and I would rather run both. Paid data tells you which keywords bring buyers within a couple of weeks, information that organic takes months to earn. Keeping them in separate silos wastes the most useful signal you have.

items.q: What does an SEO audit actually cover?
items.a: A full crawl, then a technical, on-page and content review, plus keyword and competitor gap analysis. You get a fix list ordered by impact rather than by effort, and a call where I walk you through it instead of emailing a PDF and disappearing.

items.q: Can you work with my existing site?
items.a: That is most of what I do. Technical cleanup, content structure, schema, or a migration handled without losing rankings. I can step into a build that already exists rather than insisting on starting again.

items.q: Which platforms have you worked with?
items.a: WordPress, Shopify, Magento and Strapi, among others, across e-commerce, travel, B2B services and agency portfolios. The platform changes what is easy. It almost never changes what needs fixing.

Yes. Business Profile optimisation, local pack visibility, and the service and location pages that turn a nearby search into an enquiry. For service businesses it is usually the fastest win available.

items.q: How do you report on progress?
items.a: Search Console and analytics, not screenshots of rankings. Impressions, clicks, positions, conversions, what I changed and what it moved. If a month goes badly you will hear it from me first.

items.q: Not sure what your site needs?
items.a: Send me the URL and describe the situation. Most audits and strategy calls start within 48 hours, and you will get an honest read on what is holding the site back with no pitch attached.
